newsitem.title: UK: Investors rush to buy Croatia's first Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Investors rush to buy Croatia's first Eurobond.

text.p: Croatia on Thursday raised $300 million on the international capital markets as investors eagerly snapped up the former Yugoslav republic's first bond.
"Croatia has clearly gone very well," said a syndicate manager involved in the deal.

"Croatia raised more money than they had originally planned, and could have issued an even larger bond because orders were very strong," he said. Before the bond was launched a $250 million bond was expected.
Croatia's five-year bond paid a seven percent coupon, or 0.80 percentage points more than U.S. Treasury notes. This was less than the one percentage point spread originally expected, bankers said.
The lower pricing reflected strong demand for the bond, generated by extensive roadshows across Asia, Europe and the U.S., they said.
During the presentations Croatia's finance minister Bozo Prka highlighted economic improvements since the 1995 peace settlement, signed after four years of war.
"The Croatian story is extremely good and was exceptionally well roadshowed," a banker involved in the deal said.
Croatia's economy grew 6.5 percent in real terms in 1996 and inflation was 3.5 percent, Prka told potential investors.
Growth was expected to continue at the same pace, although Croatia's fiscal deficit would rise to around 2.5 percent of GDP from one percent in 1996.
Gross borrowing in 1997 would equal around $1.0 billion, Prka said. Bankers said Croatia might tap the mark Eurobond sector next, or raise funds in the U.S. domestic Yankee market.
Croatia's bond was underwritten by U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch and by Swiss bank UBS. Officials there were not immediately available for comment.
Croatia's foreign-currency debt is rated Baa3 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB minus by IBCA and Standard & Poor's, at the lower end of the investment grade scale.
"Croatia's been very well received (by the market)," a syndicate manager at ING Barings said.
"It's an indication of European buy-side interest in a country that is close to home. Other issuers in Croatia will be coming to the market now."
